Author: @CanIBorrowYourShovel
Content:
The concierge alone on a regular ass top model iPhone (or android, let's be real, I despise apple) for an extra 2k, even if it's that combo of Ai and human... Sounds kinda worth it. Or hell, if they wanted to make that feature an app with a 200 dollar a month subscription (which chatgpt had a 200 a month option) seems like it alone would be worthwhile for a rich person. But being Chinese... You know a rich person is having all their data being tracked.

I mean the phone exterior design and the other features, if they extended them to be better than the iPhone in ways like good/equivalent speakers, display, a top tier chip that will last a good 5 years, repairability and parts availability, I could actually see myself considering one when I'm a doctor as a more long term investment. I like things that are expensive but serviceable, and nobody really makes a premium flagship/luxury phone that is. I was hoping for the hmd skyline 2 to replace my s23 ultra but consumers just suck and nobody bought the genuinely excellent skyline 1, so it didn't come to the US. 

And i just do not see the appeal of ultra luxury smart watches. Watches are a place where the wealthy can show off a hundred grand or a million if they want. And smart watches just aren't something the super wealthy even need.

And apart from phones, the idea of buying expensive but disposable versions of things that performe worse than more analog options that can 1.) show off greater wealth and taste, and 2.) last a lifetime, just doesn't make sense to me anymore. I got the Dyson zone headphones - first as a joke thinking I'd return them, but then falling in love with the sound quality, build quality and absurd anc. But then I started trying to use them in daily life. They were bulky (all over ears are) and I'm pretty sure the batteries are not user replaceable. I really didn't find them any better on a plane than my 1more Evo buds (which I actually adored the sound quality of) and when those got lost, even cheap buds, my $30 rosetechnics ceramic x buds have wind noise canceling, good enough transparency, good enough anc, no real performance issues at all, and sound better than airpod pro 2's. If I'm going to spend big money for portable performance, the cheap disposable but good enough buds, and then drop another 500+ on some extremely high end IEM's. In med school, after trying a ton of different combos of headphones earbuds and iems, I was happiest on some cheap but good anc TWS buds for the commute, and at school I switched to some $250ish apevoix grit or moondrop kadenz iems for real hifi.

Luxury tech just will never work IMO, because it's disposable.

All I know is that when I finish med school in 3 years, my one big gift to myself is not going to be a piece of tech. It's going to be a grand seiko snowflake springdrive. About 3-5k, but titanium, electeomechanical so an eerie and completely smooth second hand sweep, Japanese hand built with unique handcrafted dials meant to resemble the snow drifts in winter outside the studio window. No tech, just luxury that will last forever.

Author: @Tbonesteak23
Content:
An untold secret is that similar to Vertu, many other "highend" products that target primarily the Asian market, give it phones, or jewelry, or even floor tiles, are of Chinese origin or ownership. The real owners often start as OEM businesses and want to climb up the value chain, so they buy a niche European brand or register a foreign entity, and market themselves as a foreign highend brand or having deep & rich brand heritage. They open shops in fancy places in Paris, London, Rome or New York among other luxury brands to appear that they are one of the "old money"'s choices. There shops are there not even for selling to locals but to appeal to their target market. Vertu is definitely one of them, started as a Nokia spin-off and acquired by Chinese investor, then continues to market itself as highend British brand. Wealthy people in China, Russia, the Gulf, and parts of Southeast Asia, who often don't have much education or don't speak much English are their main target consumer groups. In China there's even a slightly offensive term dedicated for this kind of products, "智商税(IQ tax)", meaning that whoever pays for such things can't be very bright.

The situation with the website clearly shows that they don't give a f**k about the English-speaking consumers (yes there are many Chinese companies that actually sell to the whole world and the can make decent websites with proper site content), because English-speaking consumers are not their target consumer at all. The English site's sole purpose is to create an illusion of a legitimate luxury British brand.

Author: @UnpleasantAlex
Content: I once had a customer leave a Nokia Vertu on my sales desk at Best Buy in Tysons Corner. She didn’t come back to pick it up for nearly two hours. It turned out to be part of the Signature Cobra line, worth close to half a million back then, covered in diamonds, emeralds, and rubies. Underneath all that luxury, it was just a regular Nokia bar phone. I told her I’d personally hold onto it for her until she got back. Not gonna lie, a few people actually wanted me to pocket it and split the value instead of calling her. She probably never would’ve seen it again if anyone else had found it first. When she returned, I asked why anyone would buy such a basic phone with that much ornamentation, and she told me it wasn’t really about the phone at all. It was about the concierge line. Vertu gave her 24/7 lifetime access to a personal assistant service, and she said they were more efficient and dependable than any assistants she’d ever hired before. The craziest part was how calm she was about it, completely unfazed after casually misplacing half a million dollars. This was around 2006 or 2007. I wonder how different their concierge service was back then when you had to speak with a human over the phone personally compared to what they're offering now.

Author: @TheGhostInTheWires
Content: I build AI Systems for a living as a machine learning engineer/software engineer. What you are using is called a “human-in-the-loop” agent. I am building a similar system for my employer right now for our customer service department. It likely uses some kind of open source (or could be custom) framework like Parlant. It’s setup to be able to very reliably handle certain tasks on its own (they’re defined and hard coded) , and then when certain inputs are met or it can’t complete the task further, it’s handed off to a human. So for example, you send a message => it’s classified into a pre-determined subject area with its own rules for the AI agent => the AI agent converses and even makes function calls within its abilities => the bot gets to a point outside of it’s capabilities and the recorded conversation is handed off to the human who reviews it and takes over seamlessly. These system architectures are currently the most realistically usable for most business use cases because an LLM on its own is just not capable of the accuracy needed yet. But one that works within its abilities with human intervention is actually very useful for removing the more monotonous parts of customer interaction.

the thing about AI generated Arthur is
we often use these kinds of fake identities for clients, because over the course of the day you might be talking to 5 different people on the other end and we don't want to bother you with that

this is necessary so you can have 24/7 availability while we can still have a life
you can get one message from Vasily Petrenko
and then the next one from Jun Kwon because mr. Petrenko went on lunch break and the corporate doesn't want to make clients wait for an hour until he comes back
etc.

that's how we did things in a luxury tour company I worked at

these kinds of companies usually have strict guidelines for "professionalism" so we ended up sounding like bots anyway

hell they might even have a mixed setup where usually a bot answers you but whenever there's something a bot can't handle - it forwards the chat to a human
for example when it said you need to wait 20 minutes for a hotel room

Author: @MangustaMG20
Content:
I used to work for Vertu before it collapsed (at Church Crookham, Hampshire), when it operated as Vertu Corporation Ltd, now in liquidation. Back then, the marketing line “hand-assembled in England” was absolutely true — the factory had a full final-assembly line and a team of proud craftspeople.

The brand today is Chinese-based, as others have pointed out. It used to focus on high quality, which is a tough standard to maintain. In the early years Vertu products used Nokia subsystems before evolving into non-Nokia, Android-based devices, and in its later years, Vertu focused heavily on personalisation and concierge services that let clients curate their own luxury experience. Very cool back then

We also had people on the ground in a lot of major cities who could assist people who needed help.

Was a very weird job!

Author: @AlphaMachina
Content:
Vertu is currently owned by the Turkish businessman Hakan Uzan, who acquired the company in March 2017. While it was briefly owned by a Hong Kong-based fund, Godin Holdings, before Uzan's purchase, the company is not currently a Chinese-owned and run entity in the sense of being based in mainland China. 

Hakan Uzan, who lives in exile, purchased Vertu through a Cyprus-registered company named Baferton Ltd. He belongs to the controversial Uzan family, which was involved in high-profile legal battles with Nokia (Vertu's original founder) and Motorola in the early 2000s over defaulted loans and accusations of fraud. The Uzan family's substantial assets in Turkey were seized by the government as a result of these legal issues. 

Following the acquisition, the Uzan family has continued to operate the Vertu brand, although its UK-based manufacturing arm ceased operations shortly after the purchase due to debt issues. The brand was relaunched in 2018 and is now based in Hong Kong, where it continues to produce luxury mobile phones.
